name: Meroë
info: Meroë was an ancient city on the east bank of the Nile in Sudan, the southern capital of the Kingdom of Kush from around 590 BCE until the 4th century CE, and the site of more than two hundred pyramids.

facts.founded: King Aspelta moved the Kushite capital to Meroë, possibly c. 591 BCE, just after the sack of Napata by the Egyptian pharaoh Psamtik II; the city is said to have borne the older name Saba.
facts.where: On the east bank of the Nile, about 6 km north-east of the Kabushiya station and 35 km north-east of Shendi, about 200 km north-east of Khartoum, in Sudan.
facts.known: Capital of the Kingdom of Kush; the pyramids of its kings and queens; an iron industry; the Meroitic script; the war and peace of 22 BCE with Rome; the Kandake, or Queen Mother; its end in the 4th century CE
facts.today: Meroë is an archaeological site near the villages of Bagrawiyah in Sudan, listed by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site in 2011.

t: Meroë became the capital of the Kingdom of Kush around 590 BCE, when King Aspelta moved the seat of government south from Napata, and it remained the royal city for several centuries.

Its rulers drew wealth from iron, pottery, cotton and trade in ivory, gold and other goods, and from the 3rd century BCE they were buried in the pyramids at Meroë, which numbered more than two hundred.

After war with Roman Egypt and the decline of its trade, Meroë faded as a power from the 1st or 2nd century CE, and in about 350 CE it was destroyed by Axum, though some scholars point to a decline already around 300.
dyk: A head of the emperor Augustus, looted from Egypt by the Nubians, was buried under the steps of a temple at Meroë. It is now kept in the British Museum.
ev: King Aspelta moves the Kushite capital to Meroë after the sack of Napata
The royal burial ground is transferred from Napata to Meroë from the reign of Arakamani

sections.origins:
Meroë stood on the east bank of the Nile on the edge of Butana, the region bounded by the Nile, the Atbarah and the Blue Nile, which took its name as the Island of Meroë from the Kushite kingdom. The Kushite kings chose the site, between the Fifth and Sixth Cataracts, because it lay on the fringe of the summer rainfall belt, in an area rich in iron ore and hardwood for ironworking, with access to trade routes to the Red Sea.

The kingdom's first main capital was farther north at Napata. King Aspelta moved the capital to Meroë, possibly c. 591 BCE, just after the sack of Napata by Psamtik II. One account holds that the city originally bore the name Saba, after the country's original founder, and that the Persian king Cambyses gave it the name Meroë in honour of his sister. Partially deciphered Meroitic texts give its native name as Medewi.
sections.growth:
The importance of the town increased gradually from the beginning of the Meroitic Period, especially from the reign of Arakamani, c. 280 BCE, when the royal burial ground moved to Meroë from Napata. Excavations had already found high-ranking Kushite burials of the Napatan Period in the Western Cemetery near the settlement. During the third Meroitic period, which began in 270 BCE, Meroë flourished and many building projects were undertaken. At its peak its rulers controlled the Nile Valley over a straight-line distance of more than 1,000 km.

The kingdom's wealth was centred on a strong iron industry, and metalworking is believed to have taken place at Meroë. Pottery was also a widespread industry, and fine, elaborately decorated wares carried social significance and are believed to have been used in mortuary rites. Meroë traded ivory, slaves, rare skins, ostrich feathers, copper and ebony, and exported textiles and jewellery. Cotton working reached its highest achievement in Nubia around 400 BCE, and Nubia was rich in gold. The sakia was used to raise water for irrigation. After the war with Rome the period was marked by abundant trade finds at sites in Meroë.
sections.rulers:
Meroë was the southern capital of a kingdom that spanned c. 800 BCE to c. 350 CE. In the first Meroitic period (542 to 315 BCE) the kings ruled over Napata and Meroë; the seat of government and the royal palace were at Meroë, the main temple of Amun at Napata, and kings and many queens were buried at Nuri, with some queens buried in the West Cemetery at Meroë. The earliest king was Analmaye (542 to 538 BCE) and the last of the phase Nastasen (335 to 315 BCE).

In the second period, of the early 3rd century BCE, kings and many queens were buried at Meroë in the South Cemetery, and in the third period (270 BCE to the 1st century CE) kings were buried in the North Cemetery and queens in the West Cemetery. The first king of that period was Arakamani and the last ruler Queen Amanitore. In the fourth period, from the 1st to the 4th century CE, the first king was Shorkaror, and the last rulers may have been Yesebokheamani or Talakhidamani.

The king was an autocratic ruler who shared his authority only with the Queen Mother, or Kandake, whose role remains obscure. The administration included treasurers, seal bearers, heads of archives and chief scribes.
sections.life:
The Greek historian Herodotus described Meroë in the 5th century BCE as a great city said to be the mother city of the other Ethiopians. Its people worshipped southern deities such as Apedemak, the lion son of Sekhmet (or of Bast, depending on the region), and also continued to worship Egyptian gods they had brought with them, among them Amun, Tefnut, Horus, Isis, Thoth and Satis, though to a lesser extent.

The Meroitic language was spoken at Meroë and in the Sudan from at least 300 BCE and became extinct around 400 CE. It was written in two forms of the Meroitic alphabet: Meroitic Cursive, written with a stylus for general record keeping, and Meroitic Hieroglyphic, carved in stone or used for royal or religious documents. The script, of twenty-three letters, was derived from Egyptian hieroglyphs and replaced the Egyptian script by the 3rd century BCE. It is not well understood, because few bilingual texts survive, and scholars disagree whether the language belonged to the Afro-Asiatic or the Nilo-Saharan family. The Meroitic settlements of Butana lived by exploiting rainlands and savannah, and power was associated with control of people rather than of territory.
sections.crises:
Rome's conquest of Egypt led to border skirmishes and Meroitic incursions beyond the Roman frontier. In 23 BCE, in response to a Nubian attack on southern Egypt, the Roman governor Publius Petronius invaded Nubia, pillaged northern Nubia and sacked Napata in 22 BCE before returning home. In retaliation the Nubians crossed the lower border of Egypt and looted statues from the towns near the First Cataract at Aswan. Rome later reclaimed some of them, and others were returned after the peace treaty of 22 BCE between Augustus and Amanirenas.

In the autumn of 61 CE the emperor Nero sent Praetorian soldiers under a tribune and two centurions into the country. They reached Meroë, were given an escort and went up the White Nile as far as the swamps of the Sudd, the limit of Roman penetration into Africa.

The kingdom began to fade as a power by the 1st or 2nd century CE, sapped by the war with Roman Egypt and the decline of its traditional industries. The collapse of its external trade with other Nile Valley states may have been a prime cause of the decline of royal power in the 3rd and 4th centuries. In 350 CE Meroë was destroyed by Axum, and the Aksumite presence was short lived before Meroë was taken by the Kingdom of Alodia. A stele of an Aksumite king, thought to be Ezana, was found at the site. Some authorities read such inscriptions as proof that the Aksumites destroyed Kush, while others note that archaeology points to an economic and political decline around 300.
sections.legacy:
The site is marked by more than two hundred pyramids in three groups, many of them in ruins, with the distinctive size and proportions of Nubian pyramids. They were built over burial chambers holding bodies that had been burned or buried without mummification, and the chapel walls carried reliefs of queens and some kings with chapters of the Book of the Dead. Two other Meroitic cities, Musawwarat es-Sufra and Naqa, lay in Butana.

The site became known to Europeans in 1821 through the French mineralogist Frédéric Cailliaud. Giuseppe Ferlini carried out small excavations in 1834, C. R. Lepsius examined the ruins in 1844, E. A. Wallis Budge excavated in 1902 and 1905, and in 1910 J. Garstang began excavations for the University of Liverpool that found a palace and several temples. The best of the chapel reliefs were taken down in 1905 and set up in the British Museum and the museum at Khartoum. Jewish oral tradition holds that Moses, in his youth, led an Egyptian expedition to Meroë, then called Saba.

The ruins lie near the villages of Bagrawiyah, and in June 2011 the sites of Meroë were listed by UNESCO as World Heritage Sites.

summary: Meroë, on the east bank of the Nile in Sudan, became the capital of the Kingdom of Kush around 590 BCE. Its kings and queens were buried there in more than two hundred pyramids, and its iron and trade made it rich. It was destroyed in about 350 CE and is now a World Heritage site.
references: P. L. Shinnie, Meroe, a civilization of Sudan (Thames and Hudson, 1967)
notes: Source was a single article (no history article). Sections run under the 1,100 character minimum in places because the article is short; nothing padded.

START: article gives 'around 590 BC' in the lead and 'possibly c. 591 BC' for Aspelta's move; I used -591 with circa true. The article gives no founding date for the city itself; Meroitic or earlier settlement is not dated.

END: article says 'In 350 AD Meroë was destroyed by Axum' but also 'Axum ... then Meroë was taken by Alodia' and notes some authorities see decline around 300 and the Kingdom spanning to c. 350; I used 350 with endCirca true and gave both views in crises.

NAME: the article says the first site 'was given the name Meroë by the Persian king Cambyses' (the sentence is about Meroë/Musawwarat ambiguously) and that the city 'had originally borne the ancient appellation Saba'. Written as 'one account holds'. The Jewish legend also calls Meroë Saba; attributed to Jewish oral tradition. The Genesis link of Saba to a son of Cush left out.

DATES: first-period kings listed from 542 BC (Analmaye) while Napatan Period is c. 800-280 BC; First Meroitic Period header dates (542-315) and Arakamani 'c. 280 BC' (burial ground) versus Arakamani 270-260 BC (third period) differ; I used both as given in their own places (c. 280 BCE for burial move, 270 BCE for the period).
Third period said 'Meroë flourished'; I wrote 'flourished' as a plain statement of the article, not praise.

'Birmingham of Africa' and the debated iron industry (blast furnaces, 'believed' / 'possibly') left out of the text except 'believed to have taken place'; the article calls that scale a matter of debate.
The article's claims that 'Meroitic metalworkers were among the best in the world' and the Niger connection were left out as unsupported or vague.
Population, size of the city and its buildings are not given in the article; the city's layout, quarters and governance are not described, so 'life' covers faiths, language and subsistence only.
Cemeteries: the article says kings and queens are buried at Meroë 'c. 300 BC to about 350 AD'; the article also says Nuri held kings and queens in the first period.
Left out: the 2024 airstrikes on Naqa and Musawwarat es-Sufra (not Meroë itself); Periplus mention; Cailliaud's Latin inscription; Ferlini's jewellery (mentioned only the excavation).
Kandake: the article calls the Queen Mother 'Kandake' and says her role is obscure; Amanirenas and Amanitore are named as rulers without a stated title beyond 'Queen Amanitore'.
The 1821 event (Cailliaud) was dropped from ev so the last event is 350; it stays in the legacy section. Garstang is given in the article as J[ohn] Garstang.
